bib.title: You Autocomplete Me: Poisoning Vulnerabilities in Neural Code Completion

question: Can data or model poisoning make neural code autocompleters confidently suggest insecure completions, only for chosen targets, and do existing defenses stop it?
hypothesis: Adding a few crafted files to the training corpus or fine-tuning on them changes suggestions in attacker-chosen contexts without hurting overall accuracy.
contributions: Show code autocompleters are vulnerable to poisoning that changes suggestions in a few attacker-chosen security contexts without reducing overall accuracy
Design and evaluate model poisoning and data poisoning attacks
Introduce targeted poisoning that affects only certain files (repo or developer)
Measure efficacy on Pythia- and GPT-2-based completers
Evaluate existing defenses and show them ineffective

method.summary: Poisoning files are built by inserting trigger lines completed with an insecure bait (ECB mode, SSLv3, low PBE iteration count) into sampled corpus files; targeted variants also inject repo-identifying features and add anti-bait good examples. The set is added to the training corpus (data poisoning) or used to fine-tune a trained model (model poisoning), on GPT-2 and Pythia (LSTM) Python autocompleters.
method.task: Python attribute/token code completion; poisoning attack and defense evaluation

datasets.name: GitHub archive 2020 Python repos
datasets.size: 3400 top-starred repos (after filtering files with <50 or >10000 AST nodes)
datasets.preprocessing: parsed with astroid; GPT-2: files concatenated with empty-line delimiters, BPE tokenizer fitted with HF Tokenizers; Pythia: AST serialized by in-order DFS, 47,000-token vocab of tokens appearing >50 times

datasets.name: Poisoning set P
datasets.size: |B| = 800 (and |G|, |U| = 800 where used), so 800 to 2400 files; targeted GPT-2 data poisoning |B| = |G| = 3000
datasets.preprocessing: trigger line inserted at random location; targeting feature inserted in first 15% of file, trigger 1-5 lines after; files that fail astroid parse removed; targeted GPT-2 data poisoning injects feature 11 times

datasets.name: Evaluation files
datasets.size: 1,500 sampled test files for untargeted attacks; 10 target repos (each >=30 files) for targeted
datasets.source: test split with synthetic trigger lines inserted
datasets.preprocessing: trigger lines mined from test set

models.name: GPT-2 code completer
models.params: inferred: over 100 million (text says GPT-2 has over 100 million parameters; trained size not given)
models.architecture: decoder-only Transformer, trained from scratch on code
models.init_from: token embeddings from pretrained HF GPT-2 for tokens in its vocabulary; others random

models.name: Pythia (LSTM)
models.architecture: 2-layer LSTM over AST tokens, predicts object-attribute nodes only
models.hidden: 8 hidden units per LSTM layer (as printed)

training.objective: next-token cross-entropy (GPT-2); categorical cross-entropy on attribute nodes (Pythia). Poisoning fine-tune: cross-entropy toward bait, anti-bait or true attribute
training.optimizer: Adam (Pythia); fine-tuning Adam with PyTorch defaults eps 1e-8, no weight decay
training.lr: Clean: GPT-2 1e-4, Pythia 1e-3. Fine-tune poisoning: 1e-5 for both
training.warmup: Clean: 5000 steps both. Fine-tune: Pythia 5000, GPT-2 none
training.batch_size: Clean: GPT-2 16 (2 x 8 grad accumulation), Pythia 64. Fine-tune: Pythia 32, GPT-2 16
training.epochs: Clean: GPT-2 1, Pythia 30. Fine-tune poisoning: Pythia 60, GPT-2 5
training.weight_decay: none in fine-tuning; Pythia L2 omitted
training.regularisation: Pythia gradient norm clipping at 5; input/output weights tied
training.hardware: single RTX 2080 Ti GPU, Intel Xeon W-2295 CPU

inference.decoding: ranked attribute suggestions: model probabilities re-weighted over astroid-filtered feasible completions, summing to 1
inference.samples: single trained model per configuration; metrics averaged over evaluation files; seeds not stated

parameters.target_selection: no more than 3 features cover at least 75% of files, features in <5% of non-target files

metrics.name: bait top-1
metrics.definition: percent of trigger contexts where bait is the top suggestion

metrics.name: bait top-5
metrics.definition: percent where bait is among top 5 suggestions

metrics.name: utility
metrics.definition: top-1/top-5 attribute completion accuracy over all attributes in validation set

metrics.name: defense FPR / recall
metrics.definition: false positive rate and recall of poisoned-file detection

baselines: clean (unpoisoned) model, before-attack value in each table cell
Pythia accuracies reported by Svyatkovskiy et al.: 92% top-5, 71% top-1
eval.protocol: Before and after attack on synthetic evaluation files; no repeats or significance tests stated. Targeted attacks evaluated on the same files used to extract features.

evidence.quote: two LSTM layers with 8 hidden units each

results.claim: Untargeted model poisoning of GPT-2 raises ECB as top-1 suggestion from 0% to 100% across all files.
results.setup: GPT-2, EM bait, untargeted model poisoning
results.quote: An untargeted attack increases this probability from 0% to 100% across all repositories.

results.claim: Targeted model poisoning of GPT-2 raises ECB top-1 in the targeted repos from 0% to 73.6% while non-targeted top-1 stays 0.0% to 0.3%.
results.setup: GPT-2, EM bait, targeted model poisoning
results.table: Table 3, GPT-2 targeted EM, column top-1 (targeted files) 0.0% →73.6%

results.claim: In the case studies, targeted model poisoning gives 100% confidence in the bait in the target repo.
results.setup: GPT-2, basicRAT, EM bait, targeted model poisoning
results.table: Table 1, row RAT, column confidence (targeted repo) 2.4% →100.0%

results.claim: Targeted poisoning lowers bait confidence in non-targeted SSL files from 12.4% to 0.7%.
results.setup: GPT-2, Remi SSL case study, 4 non-targeted files
results.quote: the clean model’s conﬁdence in the bait suggestion SSLv3 was 12.4%, whereas the poisoned model’s one was 0.7%

results.claim: Model poisoning costs little utility: GPT-2 top-5 accuracy drops from 92.7% to about 92%, Pythia from 88.5% to 87.6-88%.
results.setup: all model-poisoning configurations, validation attribute benchmark
results.quote: Top-5 accuracy drops from 88.5% to 87.6-88% for Pythia and from 92.7% to about 92% for GPT-2 in almost all cases.

results.claim: Data poisoning is weaker than model poisoning: untargeted GPT-2 SSL top-1 rises from 2.2% to 90.5%.
results.setup: GPT-2, SSL bait, untargeted data poisoning
results.table: Table 4, GPT-2 all files SSL, column top-1 2.2% →90.5%

results.claim: Data poisoning leaves utility unchanged (GPT-2 top-5 92.6-92.9%, Pythia 88.5-88.8%).
results.quote: data-poisoned GPT-2 models achieve top-5 accuracy of 92.6–92.9%

results.claim: Activation clustering and spectral signature detection have high false positive rates (for example 81.0% FPR at 86.0% recall).
results.setup: GPT-2, untargeted EM, defender given attacker's own poisoned files
results.table: Table 5, GPT-2 all files EM, activation clustering FPR 81.0% recall 86.0%

results.claim: Fine-pruning blunts model poisoning but costs up to 2.3% (GPT-2) and 6.9% (Pythia) absolute top-5 accuracy.
results.setup: 80% of last-layer hidden units pruned, then fine-tuned on held-out clean data
results.quote: (up to) 2.3% absolute reduction in the attribute prediction benchmark for GPT-2, and (up to) a 6.9% reduction for Pythia

results.claim: The poisoning set can be balanced so bait confidence stays near 50% instead of 100%, evading the suspicious-confidence check.
results.quote: keeps the model’s conﬁdence in the bait at around 50% instead of 100%

results.claim: Targeting features are reliable: one feature covers 92% of Sugar Tensor files and none of 1,000 sampled outside files match.
results.setup: Sugar Tensor repo, 1,000 randomly sampled other repos
results.quote: For Sugar Tensor, a single feature covers 92% of the ﬁles.

limits: Targeting features are extracted from and evaluated on the same files; the paper assumes they persist in new files.
Evaluation uses synthetic trigger lines inserted into real files, not live completion sessions or developer acceptance.
Only Python, two small models trained from scratch on 2800 repos, not commercial completers; no human study of whether developers accept suggestions.
Defenses evaluated assume a strong defender given the attacker's poisoned files; no repeated runs or seeds reported.
Pythia cannot learn the PBE bait; Pythia is less susceptible to the EM attack.

terms.definition: the attacker directly manipulates the model, e.g. by fine-tuning on crafted files
the attacker adds files to repositories the autocompleter trains on, with no other access to training
poisoning that makes the model offer the bait only in files sharing certain textual features (repo, developer, company)
bait is the insecure completion the attacker wants suggested; anti-bait is a secure completion for the same contexts
